issues.legal_issue: An allottee that received land from a development board after its acquisition is not thereby a beneficiary or interested person entitled to participate in compensation proceedings or challenge the compensation award by writ, and a remand to hear such an allottee is invalid.
material_facts: The land was acquired under an industrial-development statute for the development board, and title vested in the State before the land was transferred to the board.

The board later allotted the land to a company under a lease; the lease described the premium as tentative and required the lessee to meet additional compensation payable to landowners under court awards.
The company was not identified in the acquisition notifications as the beneficiary, and the acquisition record did not establish that the land had been acquired at the company's instance.

After the Reference Court determined compensation, the company filed a writ petition challenging the award on the ground that it had not been heard; the High Court set aside the award and remanded the matter for the company to participate.
issues.conclusion: The company was only an allottee-lessee, not the beneficiary or an interested person in the acquired land for the compensation proceedings. Its writ petition challenging the award was not maintainable, and the High Court's order setting aside the award and remanding the matter to hear the company was set aside.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 28(1), 28(4)–(8), 29, 30 and 32(2) of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Act, 1966, read with Sections 3(b), 9, 11, 18, 20 and 54 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and Regulations 4, 5, 7 and 10 of the Karnataka Industrial Areas Development Board Regulations, establish that land acquired for the development board is disposed of by it under the statutory allotment process, and that an allottee-lessee does not become an interested person in the acquisition merely by receiving the land later. The Court distinguished U.P. Awas Evam Vikas v. Gyan Devi, Himalayan Tiles and Marble Pvt. Ltd. v. Francis Victor and P. Narayanappa v. State of Karnataka because those cases concerned acquisitions under the Land Acquisition Act, including acquisitions for a company or development authority. It relied on Ballarpur Industries v. Court of Civil Judge concerning the absence of a role for an allottee in compensation proceedings under the industrial-development statute.

predicates.industrial_development_acquisition_for_d: The State acquired the land for an industrial-development board under a statutory industrial-development scheme.
predicates.later_allotment_to_lessee: The development board allotted or leased the acquired land to a company after the acquisition.
predicates.lessee_challenges_compensation_award_by_: The later allottee-lessee filed a writ petition challenging the compensation award and seeking a hearing in the compensation proceedings.

issues.definition: When land is acquired for an industrial-development board and later allotted to a lessee that challenges the compensation award by writ, the allottee is not entitled to participate or challenge the award, and a remand for its hearing is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: The market value of acquired land with non-agricultural potential must reflect comparable land values and its reasonably prospective use, with deductions tailored to actual development needs rather than applied mechanically.
material_facts: The land was acquired for industrial development and had non-agricultural and commercial potential; mineral deposits in the land were used as raw material for cement manufacture.

The Reference Court relied on a valuation adopted for comparable land in the same village, but deducted development charges, waiting-period charges and conversion expenses, and also reduced the value to account for the earlier acquisition notification.
The comparable land had been acquired for industrial development and was used for a similar industrial purpose, although its acquisition notification was later and the land was some distance away.

The acquired land was used for mineral extraction and factory infrastructure, and the Court found that development activities of the kind that would justify development-charge deductions were not involved.
The landowners appealed against the compensation fixed by the Reference Court and affirmed by the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The Court allowed the landowners' appeal and re-determined the compensation at a higher market value, using the comparable land value with incidental and de-escalation deductions but without a development-charge deduction. It also awarded the applicable statutory solatium, additional amount, interest and costs.
issues.legal_principle: Section 23 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, requires market value to be assessed by reference to what a willing purchaser would pay a willing seller, considering both comparable land values and uses to which the land is reasonably capable of being put in the future. The Court relied on Raja Vyricherla Narayana Gajapatiraju v. Revenue Divisional Officer, Vizagapatam, whose principle that potential future uses may inform value was reiterated by this Court. It distinguished Chandrashekar v. Land Acquisition Officer and Another, which concerned cumulative deductions for development, de-escalation and waiting periods on different facts. Statutory benefits were awarded under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), 28 and 27 of the Land Acquisition Act.

predicates.appeal_seeks_review_of_compensation_for_: A landowner appealed a court determination of compensation for acquired land.
predicates.comparable_land_has_similar_potential_an: The evidence showed land with similar potential and a similar intended or actual use, suitable to inform the acquired land's market value.
predicates.acquired_land_has_no_comparable_developm: The acquired land was used for a purpose that did not require the development works that would justify a development-charge deduction.

issues.definition: When a compensation appeal concerns land for which comparable land has similar potential and purpose, and the acquired land does not require comparable development works, the market value is redetermined using the comparable value and fact-specific deductions, together with statutory benefits.
